CIVIL APPEAL NO. 7911/2023
HARYANA SHEHRI VIKAS PRADHIKARAN (HSVP) & ORS.  
A-1: Haryana Shehri Vikas Pradhikaran (HSVP)

Haryana Shehri Vikas Pradhikaran (HSVP)

Haryana Shehri Vikas Pradhikaran (HSVP) 
Appellant(s)
                                VERSUS
M/S. CITY VIEW ENTERPRISES                           Respondent(s)
O R D E R
Heard  Mr. Lokesh Sinhal,  learned Senior Additional Advocate
General (AAG) for the appellants and Mr. Naveen Sharma, learned
counsel for the respondent. 
2. The appellants have moved this Court against the order dated
17.04.2023  passed  by  the  National  Consumer  Dispute  Redressal
Commission at New Delhi (for short “NCDRC”) in Miscellaneous
Application No. 106 of 2021 in Consumer Complaint No. 202 of 2010.
3. Learned  Senior  AAG  for  the  appellants  submit  that  the
respondent has misused the process of the Court and the NCDRC. It
was contended that the plot in question was sold in auction to a
third party from whom the respondent had  purchased it for  a

--- Page 116 ---
2
commercial purpose.
4. It was contended that when the respondent moved the Authority
concerned for grant of a Completion Certificate of his project, the
same was refused primarily on the ground that there were zoning
violations which were of a nature which could not be condoned or
compounded.  However,  it  was  submitted  that  surprisingly,  the
respondent moved before the NCDRC which, by a detailed and reasoned
order dated 01.02.2016, passed by a quorum of two Members of the
NCDRC, had dismissed the claim, holding that the respondent was not
a consumer in view of the matter  relating to purchase of a
commercial plot in a public auction and rejection of the Occupancy
Certificate in respect of a commercial building constructed on such
plot.
5. Learned counsel submitted that there was no infirmity in the
order and the respondent had also accepted the same as for five
years,  he  did  not  move  against  the  said  order.  However,
surprisingly, according to the learned counsel, in the year 2021
M.A. No. 106 of 2021 was filed for Direction in the said case,
which already stood disposed of. The said M.A. was pending and in
the meantime, this Court in CA No. 236 of 2022 by order dated
07.01.2022 had observed that such M.A. would not be maintainable
before the NCDRC in a disposed of matter. It was contended that
despite all this, by the impugned order, the order dated 01.02.2016
was recalled, the  M.A. filed by the respondent was allowed and
consequently the earlier order dated 01.02.2016 was recalled and a
direction  was  issued  to  the  Authorities  to  issue

--- Page 117 ---
3
Occupancy/Completion Certificate to the respondent.
6. Learned counsel submitted that the order is in the teeth of
not only statutory provisions, but also the order of this Court in
CA No. 236 of 2022. It was further contended that even on facts,
because  of  there  being  violation  of  zoning  regulations,  no
indulgence can be shown to the respondent.
7. Learned counsel for the respondent submitted that the NCDRC in
its order dated 01.02.2016, had erroneously held that it was a
commercial transaction and the respondent was not a consumer,
whereas the fact is that he is a consumer as ultimately, it is to
individual parties that the built up space has been sold and thus
the respondent can act on their behalf in representative capacity.
8. While winding up his argument, the learned counsel for the
respondent submitted that as of now, there is a scheme floated by
the State of Haryana under which the prayer of the respondent can
be considered under which he has already applied.
9. Having considered the matter, we find that the order impugned
dated 01.02.2016, passed by the NCDRC in Consumer Case No. 202 of
2010, is well reasoned and did not suffer from any infirmity, much
less could have been reversed on the basis of a Miscellaneous
Application filed by the respondent. Further, we find that the
cause  of  action  to  the  respondent  against  the  order  dated
01.02.2016, not being agitated before the appropriate forum for
five years itself was a ground for his M.A. to be rejected
outright. We also note here that in the M.A., the reliefs claimed

--- Page 118 ---
4
for are substantially new and different from what was the original
prayer made in Consumer Case No. 202 of 2010.
10. Thus, we find that the very inception of the proceedings,
which was before the NCDRC was misconceived.
11. Accordingly, for the reasons aforesaid, the appeal is allowed.
The  order  impugned  dated  17.04.2023  passed  by  the  NCDRC  in
Miscellaneous Application No. 106 of 2021 in Consumer Complaint No.
202 of 2010 is set aside. The order of the NCDRC dated 01.02.2016
in Consumer Case No.202 of 2010 stands revived.
12. It shall be open to the respondent to move before the
appropriate forum, in accordance with law, for any grievance he may
have which shall be considered on its own merit, in accordance with
law.
13. Pending applications, if any, stand disposed of.
......................J.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CIVIL APPEAL NO. 7911/2023
HARYANA SHEHRI VIKAS PRADHIKARAN (HSVP) & ORS.  
  
A-1: Haryana Shehri Vikas Pradhikaran (HSVP) 
A-2: The Administrator, 
Haryana Shehri Vikas Pradhikaran (HSVP) 
A-3: The Estate Officer, 
Haryana Shehri Vikas Pradhikaran (HSVP) 
Appellant(s)
                                VERSUS
M/S. CITY VIEW ENTERPRISES                           Respondent(s)
O R D E R
Heard  Mr. Lokesh Sinhal,  learned Senior Additional Advocate
General (AAG) for the appellants and Mr. Naveen Sharma, learned
counsel for the respondent. 
2. Leave granted.
3. The appellants have moved this Court against the order dated
17.04.2023  passed  by  the  National  Consumer  Dispute  Redressal
Commission at New Delhi (for short “NCDRC”) in Miscellaneous
Application No. 106 of 2021 in Consumer Complaint No. 202 of 2010.
4. Learned  Senior  AAG  for  the  appellants  submit  that  the
respondent has misused the process of the Court and the NCDRC. It
was contended that the plot in question was sold in auction to a

--- Page 122 ---
8
third party from whom the respondent had  purchased it for  a
commercial purpose.
5. It was contended that when the respondent moved the Authority
concerned for grant of a Completion Certificate of his project, the
same was refused primarily on the ground that there were zoning
violations which were of a nature which could not be condoned or
compounded.  However,  it  was  submitted  that  surprisingly,  the
respondent moved before the NCDRC which, by a detailed and reasoned
order dated 01.02.2016, passed by a quorum of two Members of the
NCDRC, had dismissed the claim, holding that the respondent was not
a consumer in view of the matter  relating to purchase of a
commercial plot in a public auction and rejection of the Occupancy
Certificate in respect of a commercial building constructed on such
plot.
6. Learned counsel submitted that there was no infirmity in the
order and the respondent had also accepted the same as for five
years,  he  did  not  move  against  the  said  order.  However,
surprisingly, according to the learned counsel, in the year 2021
M.A. No. 106 of 2021 was filed for Direction in the said case,
which already stood disposed of. The said M.A. was pending and in
the meantime, this Court in CA No. 236 of 2022 by order dated
07.01.2022 had observed that such M.A. would not be maintainable
before the NCDRC in a disposed of matter. It was contended that
despite all this, by the impugned order, the order dated 01.02.2016
was recalled, the  M.A. filed by the respondent was allowed and
consequently the earlier order dated 01.02.2016 was recalled and a

--- Page 123 ---
9
direction  was  issued  to  the  Authorities  to  issue
Occupancy/Completion Certificate to the respondent.
7. Learned counsel submitted that the order is in the teeth of
not only statutory provisions, but also the order of this Court in
CA No. 236 of 2022. It was further contended that even on facts,
because  of  there  being  violation  of  zoning  regulations,  no
indulgence can be shown to the respondent.
8. Learned counsel for the respondent submitted that the NCDRC in
its order dated 01.02.2016, had erroneously held that it was a
commercial transaction and the respondent was not a consumer,
whereas the fact is that he is a consumer as ultimately, it is to
individual parties that the built up space has been sold and thus
the respondent can act on their behalf in representative capacity.
9. While winding up his argument, the learned counsel for the
respondent submitted that as of now, there is a scheme floated by
the State of Haryana under which the prayer of the respondent can
be considered under which he has already applied.
10. Having considered the matter, we find that the order impugned
dated 01.02.2016, passed by the NCDRC in Consumer Case No. 202 of
2010, is well reasoned and did not suffer from any infirmity, much
less could have been reversed on the basis of a Miscellaneous
Application filed by the respondent. Further, we find that the
cause  of  action  to  the  respondent  against  the  order  dated
01.02.2016, not being agitated before the appropriate forum for
five years itself was a ground for his M.A. to be rejected

--- Page 124 ---
10
outright. We also note here that in the M.A., the reliefs claimed
for are substantially new and different from what was the original
prayer made in Consumer Case No. 202 of 2010.
11. Thus, we find that the very inception of the proceedings,
which was before the NCDRC was misconceived.
12. Accordingly, for the reasons aforesaid, the appeal is allowed.
The  order  impugned  dated  17.04.2023  passed  by  the  NCDRC  in
Miscellaneous Application No. 106 of 2021 in Consumer Complaint No.
202 of 2010 is set aside. The order of the NCDRC dated 01.02.2016
in Consumer Case No.202 of 2010 stands revived.
13. It shall be open to the respondent to move before the
appropriate forum, in accordance with law, for any grievance he may
have which shall be considered on its own merit, in accordance with
law.
14. Pending applications, if any, stand disposed of.

[Arising out of impugned final judgment and order dated  10-04-2024
in WA No. 24996/2018 passed by the High Court of Judicature at

JAGDISH PRASAD TRIPATHI                              Petitioner(s)
                                VERSUS
STATE OF U.P. THROUGH ITS PRINCIPAL SECRETARY & ORS. Respondent(s)
(IA No. 197066/2026 - CONDONATION OF DELAY IN FILING)
 
Date : 01-10-2026 This matter was called on for hearing today.
CORAM : 
         HON'BLE MR. JUSTICE K.V. VISWANATHAN
         HON'BLE MR. JUSTICE ARUN PALLI
For Petitioner(s)  Ms. Anita Tripathi, Sr. Adv.
                   Mr. Umesh Dubey, AOR
                   Mr. Anshuman Tripathi, Adv.
                   Mr. Mohnish Nirwan, Adv.
                   Mr. Ashok Kumar, Adv.
                   Mr. Mithilesh Kumar Mishra, Adv.
                   Mr. Sudhanshu Tiwari, Adv.
                  
For Respondent(s) : Ms. Ruchira Goel- 2477, AOR
                   
          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
Delay condoned.
1. This is a very unfortunate case.  The petitioner was
appointed in the year 1984 to the post of Peon in the Jan
Sevak Uchchattar Madhyamik Vidyalaya, Para Basupur Akhand
Nagar, District-Sultanpur. After a long service of nearly
thirty-two years, petitioner superannuated on 31.07.2016.
Petitioner’s service was a pensionable service. Petitioner
made a request to release his pension repeatedly. The

--- Page 162 ---
2
petitioner  filed  a  complaint  online  to  the  District
Magistrate, Sultanpur on 17.03.2018. Subsequently, also
several complaints were filed.
2. Left with no other option on 29.08.2018, petitioner
filed Writ Application No.24996/2018 before the High Court
of judicature at Allahabad, Lucknow Bench, Lucknow for
payment of retiral benefits.
3. The matter was pending in the High Court and on
17.04.2023 an order was made to list the case in the week
commencing 15.05.2023. Thereafter the matter was taken up
on 10.04.2024 wherein the Court directed the Office to
trace and place on record the short counter affidavit
filed by the State. After the hearing on 10.04.2024, the
case was not listed thereafter.
4. On 08.10.2025, the petitioner filed C.M. Application
No.181662 of 2025 in the pending writ petition for early
hearing and disposal of the Writ Petition. It transpires
that  on  30.04.2026  that  application  was  disposed  of
without fixing any date. The petitioner then filed a
Special Leave Petition before this Court challenging the
order of 10.04.2024 which had directed the tracing out of
the counter affidavit and placing it on the record.
5. The matter came up before us and when we read
through the records, we were shocked to know that for the
last ten years after superannuation for no fault of the
petitioner, the petitioner has not been paid his retiral

--- Page 163 ---
3
dues. Though the order impugned was only an order fixing a
date and though we do not interfere with such orders,
considering  the  fact  that  the  issue  pertains  to  the
livelihood of and dignity of the petitioner, we issued
notice  to  the  State  and  requested  Ms.  Ruchira  Goel,
learned standing counsel to obtain instructions and assist
us at the next date of hearing. 
6. We were also informed by Ms. Anita Tripathi, learned
senior counsel for the petitioner that after nine years in
2025, the gratuity amount alone was paid. 
7. Ms. Ruchira Goel, learned senior counsel acted with
promptitude  and  made  sure  that  the  State  filed  a
compliance  affidavit  dated  08.09.2026.  The  compliance
affidavit first set out that since the petitioner was
absent between 20.07.2009 and 30.11.2010 only provisional
pension had been approved. It was also averred that after
approval of the provisional pension, the petitioner was
requested  to  submit  relevant  documents  and  that  the
petitioner did not respond. In the very next paragraph
(paragraph 12), it is averred that the petitioner salary
was indeed paid between 20.07.2009 and 30.11.2010 and that
there was no interruption from service.
8. Paragraph Nos. 11 and 12 of the compliance affidavit
are set out hereinbelow:
“11. It is submitted that the Petitioner was absent
from 20.07.2009 to 30.11.2010, and his service was
interrupted, as a result of which only provisional

--- Page 164 ---
4
pension had been approved by the then District basic
Education Officer, Sultanpur. After approval of the
provisional pension, the Petitioner was repeatedly
requested to submit the relevant documents so that
the provisional pension due could be paid. However,
the petitioner neither responded to such requests,
nor appeared personally.
12. It is submitted that after examination of the
Petitioner’s file by the Block Education Officer,
Bhadaiya  Sultanpur,  it  was  observed  that  the
Petitioner’s salary for the period between 20.07.2009
and 30.11.2010 was paid, indicating there was no
interruption in service. In view thereof, vide Letter
No.Non-Govt. Sec./11803-11/2026-27, dated 06.08.2026.
District Basic Education Officer, Sultanpur cancelled
the  previously  approved  provisional  pension  and
granted a recommendation for final pension. After
verification of the Petitioner’s file, the same has
been forwarded to the Additional Director, Treasury

1. Delay of 108 days in re-filing is condoned. Permission to

2. The  instant  Writ  Petition,  filed  purportedly  in  public

(a) ISSUE AN APPROPRIATE WRIT, ORDER OR DIRECTION IN THE

DECLARING-
(i)  that Articles 14 and 21, read with Article 39-A of
the Constitution of India, require that the reliance by
the State upon forensic, scientific, digital or Al-
derived evidence to restrict the personal liberty of a
person be attended by a corresponding constitutional
entitlement in the person so affected; and (ii) that the
said  entitlement  consists  in  an  enforceable  and
practical means of independently examining, verifying
and contesting the scientific conclusions so relied
upon;
(b)  ISSUE AN APPROPRIATE WRIT, ORDER OR DIRECTION IN

proceedings is constitutionally deficient to the extent
that it provides no such mechanism, it being expressly
clarified that the Petitioner does not challenge the
constitutional validity of any statutory provision;

3. The petitioner contends that the BNSS and the BSA vest the
6

--- Page 183 ---
entire forensic process in the State, while giving the accused no
corresponding right of access to the material underlying a forensic
conclusion,  of  independent  re-examination,  or  to  have  the
reliability of the method scrutinised; that safeguards at every
stage are thus available only to the State and none to the accused,
which he describes as a failure of the “Doctrine of Forensic
Equality” and as offending Articles 14, 21 and 39-A of the
Constitution. He further cautions against reliance on AI-assisted
identification tools used without disclosure of their accuracy,
error rates or methodology, which, according to him, offends
Articles 14 and 21. Moreover, he submits that State forensic
laboratories  are  not  independent  of  the  executive  hierarchy
supervising investigation, and that legal aid under the Legal
Services Authorities Act, 1987 does not extend to the cost of
independent forensic examination. The petitioner clarifies that he
does not challenge the validity of any statutory provision.
4. In this regard,  the petitioner states that he has already
represented before the relevant authorities. We, therefore, without
expressing any opinion on the merits, dispose of this petition with
liberty to the petitioner to pursue the cause before the competent
authorities, including by way of his representations already made.
The petitioner shall, within two weeks from today, deposit the
requisite court fee of the paper book with the Registry of this
Court, whereupon a copy of this Writ Petition shall be forwarded to
the respondent(s) for their consideration in accordance with law.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CIVIL ORIGINAL JURISDICTION
ARBITRATION PETITION (C) No.43 OF 2017
M/S RUBY CHEMICALS          … PETITIONER
VERSUS
M/S. ROBERTET SA                    … RESPONDENT
O  R  D  E  R
1. The present petition seeking appointment of arbitrator under Section 11(6) of the
Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 (`the Act’) raises a piquant state of affairs. 
2. Admittedly, M/s Robertet SA (‘Respondent’), formerly M/s Charabot Group, entered
into an agreement on 19.04.1995 with M/s Ruby Chemicals (‘Petitioner’) which was signed
by the Petitioner’s proprietor on 23.04.1995 for purchase of aleuritic acid and its derivatives.
The agreement contained an arbitration clause which reads as follows: 
"All disputes arising in connection with this agreement shall be
finally settled under the rules of conciliation and arbitration of the
International Chamber of Commerce by one or more Arbitrators
appointed in accordance with the said Rules".
3. Disputes and differences arose between the parties in respect of the said agreement
prompting the Petitioner to file a suit before the High Court at Calcutta (CS No.622/2001).
The Respondent took out an application under Section 8 of the Arbitration and Conciliation
Act, 1996 (A.P. No. 14 of 2003), which came to be allowed vide order dated 01.12.2003.

--- Page 194 ---
2
4. Thereafter, on 17.04.2008 the Petitioner made a request for arbitration before the
International Chamber of Commerce (‘ICC’) under the ICC Arbitration Rules, 1998 (‘ICC
Rules’). By letter dated 23.04.2009, ICC fixed advance on costs and recorded that the
Petitioner had paid a sum of USD 70,000 as provisional advance on costs. By subsequent
emails dated 13.07.2009 and 18.08.2009, the Secretariat of ICC intimated the Petitioner to
put in the remainder of its share on advance on costs while also recording that the
Respondent had not put in its share. It further directed that in the event the Respondent fails
to do so, the liability would be borne by the Petitioner through substitution.  Learned counsel
for the Petitioner contends that due to non-cooperation of the Respondent in putting in its
share of advance on costs, the arbitration proceeding before ICC failed to take off and stood
withdrawn on 12.02.2010. In this backdrop, his client was constrained to take out an
application under Section 11(6) of the Act for appointment of an arbitrator, which was
initially disposed of by this Court vide order dated 24.10.2017 holding that the arbitration
proceedings before ICC has since proved abortive, and the Petitioner would be permitted to
pursue the suit (CS 622 of 2001). Such order, having been passed without notice to the
Respondent, came to be recalled vide order dated 23.01.2026 and the matter was placed
for fresh hearing. 
5. Mr. Ritin Rai, learned Senior Counsel for the Respondent refers to Article 30 of the
ICC Rules and contends that the default on advance of costs lay not only with the
Respondent, but was also, in part, attributable to the Petitioner. In the alternate, he
contends that it was open to the Petitioner to put in the costs on behalf of the Respondent
and recover the same at an appropriate stage. Even post withdrawal, the same claim could
be re-introduced in another proceeding under the ICC Rules.  According to him, such state
of affairs had not been correctly portrayed before the court earlier, and had led to the revival
of the suit, which is impermissible in law. 

--- Page 195 ---
3
6. We have considered Mr. Rai’s submission in light of the material on record.
Admittedly, the suit instituted by the Petitioner in the Calcutta High Court had been referred
to arbitration under ICC Rules. The Petitioner accepted the order and had proceeded for
arbitration before the ICC. Such endeavour, however, was rendered futile as the advance
on costs were not fully paid. The Petitioner contends that such failure was primarily on
account of the Respondent not putting in its costs. Contrarily, the Respondent argues that
the Petitioner itself had not discharged its liability fully or resorted to Article 30 (3) of the ICC
Rules to put in the costs entirely and subsequently recover it at an appropriate stage. 
7. The emails exchanged between the Petitioner and ICC show that the Petitioner had
initially deposited a portion of the advance on costs. However, considering the unwillingness
of the Respondent to deposit its share, the Petitioner refrained from putting in the remaining
portion of its share resulting in withdrawal of the proceeding. 
8. Mr. Rai argues that such withdrawal would not result in an exhaustion of the
arbitration clause and therefore the arbitration could still be revived in terms of Article 30 (4).
9. For better appreciation of such argument, Article 30 is set out hereinbelow:
“1
After receipt of the Request, the Secretary General may request
the Claimant to pay a provisional advance in an amount
intended to cover the costs of arbitration until the Terms of
Reference have been drawn up.
2
As soon as practicable, the Court shall fix the advance on costs
in an amount likely to cover the fees and expenses of the
arbitrators and the ICC administrative costs for the claims and
counterclaims which have been referred to it by the parties. This
amount may be subject to readjustment at any time during the
arbitration. Where, apart from the claims, counterclaims are
submitted, the Court may fix separate advances on costs for the
claims and the counterclaims.
3

--- Page 196 ---
4
The advance on costs fixed by the Court shall be payable in
equal shares by the Claimant and the Respondent. Any
provisional advance paid on the basis of Article 30(1) will be
considered as a partial payment thereof. However, any party
shall be free to pay the whole of the advance on costs in respect
of the principal claim or the counterclaim should the other party
fail to pay its share. When the Court has set separate advances
on costs in accordance with Article 30(2), each of the parties
shall pay the advance on costs corresponding to its claims.
4
When a request for an advance on costs has not been complied
with, and after consultation with the Arbitral Tribunal, the
Secretary General may direct the Arbitral Tribunal to suspend its
work and set a time limit, which must be not less than 15 days,
on the expiry of which the relevant claims, or counterclaims,
shall be considered as withdrawn. Should the party in question
wish to object to this measure, it must make a request within the
aforementioned period for the matter to be decided by the Court.
Such party shall not be prevented, on the ground of such
withdrawal, from reintroducing the same claims or counterclaims
at a later date in another proceeding.
5
If one of the parties claims a right to a set-off with regard to
either claims or counterclaims, such set-off shall be taken into
account in determining the advance to cover the costs of
arbitration in the same way as a separate claim insofar as it may
require the Arbitral Tribunal to consider additional matters.”
10. The scheme laid down under Article 30 reveals that initially the Secretary General
may call upon the claimant to put in a provisional sum to cover the costs of arbitration till
terms of reference are drawn up. Thereupon, the Court fixes the advance on costs for fees,
the expenses of arbitrators as well as arbitration costs, and the parties are to pay the said
advance on costs within the stipulated time. In the event of failure to do so, the Secretary
General shall direct the arbitrator to suspend work along with withdrawal of the claims and
Counter claims. If a party fails to pay its share, the other party is free to pay the whole of the
advance on costs in respect of the claim/counter claim. Withdrawal of any claim/counter
claim due to non-payment of advance on costs, as aforesaid, would not pre-empt the party
from reintroducing the same claim or counterclaim at a later date in another proceeding. 

--- Page 197 ---
5
11. There is no dispute that while the Petitioner had put in the provisional cost of USD
70,000, the remainder of the advance on costs assessed at USD 305,000 remained unpaid.
Consequently, the arbitration proceeding had stood withdrawn.
 
12. The moot issue which falls for consideration is whether such proceeding is required
to be reintroduced in another proceeding under the ICC Rules or it is open to the parties to
raise such claim before any other alternative forum, including a Court of law. 
13. While party autonomy is the heart and soul of arbitration law, the question whether a
party is bound to proceed for arbitration before the forum where the claim had stood
withdrawn due to non-cooperation by the other party to put in its share of costs, must be
understood in the backdrop of the fundamental right of access to justice. 
14. As recounted earlier, in the present case, the Respondent’s failure to put in its share
of advance on costs, had cast an onerous burden on the Petitioner to shoulder the entire
amount of advance on costs. As the Petitioner failed to arrange the entire advance on costs,
it was faced with the inevitable withdrawal of its claims. Mr. Rai argues that Petitioner was
fully aware of such liability and was not barred from reintroducing such claim before the
ICC.  We are unwilling to accept such averment at the behest of the Respondent who has
resorted to an obstructionist approach before all fora to defeat the adjudication of the claims
on merit.  Firstly, in the civil suit instituted by the Petitioner before the Calcutta High Court,
the Respondent prayed that the parties may be referred to arbitration. When the matter
came to be referred to ICC for arbitration, the Respondent chose to derail such exercise by
not putting in its share of costs. At the time of entering into the agreement, it was never
contemplated by the Petitioner that the Respondent would blow hot and cold and scuttle the
arbitration by not depositing his share of costs. It is true that under such circumstances the
Petitioner could have put in the whole costs and proceeded with the arbitration. However,
such a step, bearing in mind the hardships and complexities in arranging foreign exchange

--- Page 198 ---
6
etc., would require the Petitioner to discharge an extremely onerous if not insurmountable
burden, rendering the adjudicatory mechanism illusory for all practical purposes.
15. The Respondent’s contention that he did not put in his share as the Petitioner’s claim
was inflated is most specious and inspires no confidence as the parties were to pay the
advance on costs in equal share and no higher burden was placed on the Respondent as
compared to that on the Petitioner. 
16. Keeping in mind the obdurate refusal of the Respondent to deposit its share of
advance on costs, we are of the considered view that any reference to fresh arbitration
under Article 30(4) of the ICC Rules for reintroduction of the said claim would be futile and
meet the same abortive end. 
17. However, such obtuse stance of the Respondent cannot render the Petitioner
remediless on account of his inability to arrange foreign exchange and deposit the whole
advance on costs for arbitration. Accordingly, in order to balance equities and do complete
justice, we invoke Article 142 and direct as follows:
(i) As the arbitration arrangement between the parties is rendered unworkable at
the behest of the Respondent, Petitioner is at liberty to institute a commercial
suit before the Commercial Court of competent jurisdiction within 30 days,
without recourse to pre-litigation mediation under Section 12A of the
Commercial Courts Act, 2015. 
(ii) All other issues, including limitation, are kept open for adjudication by the said
Commercial Court in accordance with law and in view of the observations
made in this order.
18. The Arbitration Petition stands disposed of accordingly.

--- Page 199 ---
7
19. As a result, the pending interlocutory application also stands disposed of.
 
           ..………..….....……………….…....J.
      (JOYMALYA BAGCHI)
           ..………..….....……………….…....J.
      (V. MOHANA)
NEW DELHI

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION 
Civil Appeal No(s).      /2026
@ SLP (C) No. 3100/2026
MANOJ SANJAY DESHPANDE                       Appellant(s)
VERSUS
RAJENDRA DHARMA  JADHAV & ORS.              Respondent(s)
O R D E R
1. Leave granted.
2. Heard learned counsel for the parties.
3. This appeal impugns the judgment and order of
the  High  Court  of  Judicature  at  Bombay  dated
09.12.2025 passed in W.P. No. 1577/2022 and Interim
Application No. 804/2022.
4. Writ proceedings before the High Court were
in the context of a change report relating to the
management of a Trust for the period 2016-2019. The
High Court after considering the submissions of the
learned counsel for the parties took the view that
1

--- Page 202 ---
as three-year period had admittedly expired, a fresh
inquiry  under  Section  22  would  be  required  to
appoint nine persons as members of the Management
Committee of the Trust. The High Court thus directed
the Joint Charity Commissioner to conduct a fresh
inquiry under Section 22 and appoint nine persons as
members of the Managing Committee of the Trust in
accordance  with  law  and  by  following  the  due
process.
5. The appellants have challenged the aforesaid
order on the ground that after the term of the
earlier Committee was over in the year 2019, a fresh
election had taken place constituting a new Managing
Committee of which a change report was submitted to
the Assistant Charity Commissioner. It is submitted
that the Assistant Charity Commissioner has accepted
the change report and aggrieved by such acceptance,
the aggrieved parties are in appeal before the Joint
Charity Commissioner by way of Trust Appeal Nos. 83-
84/2023. In such circumstances, according to the
appellants, there was no justification to issue a
2

--- Page 203 ---
direction  to  the  Joint  Charity  Commissioner  to
conduct an inquiry and appoint nine persons as
members of the Managing Committee. 
6. Based  on  the  aforesaid  submissions,  on
27.01.2026 we had passed the following order:
“1.  The  submission  of  the  learned
counsel for the petitioner is that the
High Court did not decide the issue on
merits as 3 years’ period for which the
election was held had already lapsed.
However, while disposing of the writ
petition, the High Court directed the
Joint Charity Commissioner to conduct a
fresh  inquiry  under  Section  22  and
appoint nine members Managing Committee
of the Trust. It is submitted that in
the  interregnum  fresh  elections  had
been held and the change report was
also accepted and, therefore, there was
no occasion to direct the Joint Charity
Commissioner  to  conduct  an  inquiry
under  Section  22  and  appoint  nine
members  Managing  Committee  of  the
Trust.
2.  Issue  notice,  returnable  in  six
weeks.
3. In the meantime, the direction of
the High Court to the Joint Charity
Commissioner  to  conduct  an  inquiry
under  Section  22  and  appoint  nine
members Managing Committee shall remain
stayed.” 
7. Pursuant  to  the  notice,  the  respondents  have
appeared through counsel.
8. The learned counsel for the respondents submits
3

--- Page 204 ---
that the order of the High Court may be set aside and
parties may be allowed to contest their case in the
appeal(s)  pending  before  the  Joint  Charity
Commissioner.
9. The learned Counsel for the appellants has no issue
in accepting the aforesaid proposal.
10. In view of the above, we deem it appropriate to
set aside the impugned order dated 09.12.2025 and
relegate  the  parties  to  pursue  their  respective
appeal(s)  pending  before  the  Joint  Charity
Commissioner, Nashik Region.
11. Accordingly, this appeal is allowed. The order
impugned dated 09.12.2025 is set aside. The rights of

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION 
Criminal Appeal No(s).      /2026
@ SLP (Crl) No. 13293/2026
ANU ANIL NAIR                                Appellant(s)
                                VERSUS
STATE OF KERALA & ANR.                      Respondent(s)
O R D E R
1. Leave granted.
2. Heard learned counsel for the parties.
3. This appeal impugns the judgment and order of the
High Court of Kerala at Ernakulam dated 10.06.2026
by which the High Court has declined to quash the
proceedings  emanating  from  Crime  No.706/2024
registered at P.S. Kalamassery under Sections 354,
354(A)(1)(ii), 354B, 376, 509 and 451 of the Indian
Penal Code, 1860 which are now pending as C.P.
No.5/2025 in the Court of Judicial First Class
Magistrate, Kalamassery.
1

--- Page 209 ---
4. The  appellant  and  the  second  respondent  were
formerly engaged to get married. The marriage could
not take place, and a complaint came to be lodged
at the instance of the second respondent wherein it
was alleged that she was sexually exploited by the
appellant. The parties, however, resolved their
differences and, ultimately, based on a compromise,
prayed for quashing of the proceedings by invoking
the inherent powers of the High Court.
5. The High Court declined the prayer of quashing of
the proceedings on the ground that an offence
concerning sexual assault falls in the category of
heinous offences which cannot be quashed based on a
compromise.
6. Aggrieved by the order of the High Court, this
appeal has been filed.
7. On 31.07.2026, after considering the submissions of
the learned counsel for the appellant, we had
passed the following order:
2

--- Page 210 ---
“1.  The  submission  of  the  learned
counsel for the petitioner is that the
prosecutrix  and  the  petitioner  were
formally  engaged  to  get  married.
However,  on  account  of  certain
differences  between  them  a  First
Information Report (FIR) was lodged by
the prosecutrix alleging sexual assault
on her by the petitioner at her house.
Later, the differences were resolved
and an affidavit was presented by the
prosecutirx  before  the  High  Court
agreeing for quashment of the FIR and
the consequential proceedings as they
were  instituted  on  account  of  some
misunderstanding between them. 
2.  Considering  the  nature  of  the
offences, the High Court declined the
prayer to quash the FIR.
3. The submission on behalf of the
petitioner is that this is not a case
of usual rape but it is a case of
alleged physical relationship between
two persons who were formally engaged
to get married and, therefore, basis a
settlement,  the  proceedings  can  be
quashed to ensure that there is no
abuse of the process of law. Moreover,
it is a case where the prosecutrix
herself would be the witness and if she
is not wiling to come forward, the
trial would be an exercise in futility.
4.  Issue  notice,  returnable  in  six
weeks.  5.  Notice  on  behalf  of
respondent no.2 has been accepted by
3

--- Page 211 ---
Mr.  Jogy  Scaria,  AOR  6.  In  the
meantime, further proceedings emanating
from FIR No.706/2024 dated 23.07.2024
registered  at  P.S.  Kalamassery,
District Ernakulum City, Kerala shall
remain stayed.”
8. Pursuant to the above order, the respondents are
represented.
9. The  second  respondent,  who  happens  to  be  the
complainant, is represented through her Counsel.
10. The  learned  counsel  representing  the  second
respondent submits that he would have no objection
if the proceedings are quashed on the basis of the
compromise between the parties.
11. Having regard to the background facts of the case
and the relationship between the parties prior to
the alleged incident of sexual assault, we are of
the view that this is a peculiar case which cannot
be  equated  with  a  case  of  sexual  assault
simpliciter. Here the parties were engaged to get
married and during that relationship some incident
occurred which was reported.
4

--- Page 212 ---
12. In  such  circumstances,  when  the  parties  have
resolved their differences and have prayed for
quashing of the proceedings, no useful purpose
would be served by continuing those proceedings
particularly when the relationship of the parties
permitted them to be in company of each other. We,
therefore, deem it appropriate to invoke our powers
under Article 142 of the Constitution of India and
quash the proceedings emanating from Crime No.
706/2024(supra).
13. Accordingly, this appeal is allowed. The order of
the High Court dated 10.06.2026 is hereby set
aside. The proceedings emanating from Case Crime
No. 706/2024 registered at P.S. Kalamassery are
hereby quashed based on a settlement between the
parties.
14. Pending  application(s),  if  any,  shall  stand
disposed of.

1. The present petition calls in question the correctness of

2
Allahabad.
2. The petitioners filed the petition under Section 528 of
the  Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita ( for short, ‘BNSS’)
seeking  to  quash  and  set  aside  the  chargesheet  dated
29.10.2024 filed under Section 3(1) & 2(b)(xv) of the Uttar
Pradesh Gangsters and Anti-Social Activities (Prevention) Act,
1986 (for short, ‘UP Gangsters Act’) arising out of Case Crime
No.23/2024, registered at Police Station Nizamabad, District
Azamgarh, Uttar Pradesh as well as seeking quashment of the
cognizance  of  the  orders  dated  16.12.2024  and  04.04.2025
passed  by  learned  Additional  District  &  Sessions  Judge,
Special Judge, (Gangsters Act) Court No.6, Azamgarh, Uttar
Pradesh  (for  short,  ‘Special  Judge  at  Azamgarh’).  The
petitioners  also challenged  the non-bailable  warrants and
proclamation  under  Section  82  of  the  Code  of  Criminal
Procedure, 1973 (for short, ‘CRPC’) as well as the entire
criminal proceedings arising out of Special Sessions Trial
No.161/2024 under Section 3(1) of the UP Gangsters Act pending
before the Special Judge at Azamgarh.
3. The  High  Court,  by  a  short  order,  disposed  of  the
petition/application, the operative portion of which reads
thus:-
“Considering the facts and circumstances of the matter,
applicant is directed to appear before the learned
Court  concerned  in  pursuance  to  proceeding  under
challenge within three weeks from today. Till three
weeks from today, no coercive action shall be initiated

--- Page 223 ---
3
against the applicant. After the expiry of aforesaid
period of three weeks, learned concerned Court is
directed to proceed as per law.”
4. The petitioners aggrieved, filed the present Special

proceedings in Special Sessions Trial No.161/2024 arising out
of  Case  Crime  No.23/2024,  registered  at  Police  Station
Nizamabad, District Azamgarh, Uttar Pradesh.

State-respondents.

to the base case, namely, FIR No.469/2023 registered at Police

7. The First Information Report of the said case reads as
under:-
“XXXXX
To, Shriman Thanadhyaksha Sir, Police Station Nizamabad

not understand and beef was present in the bag and I

have an old dispute with my neighbour Saheb Alam son of

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CIVIL APPEAL NO.8867/2013
D.T. ANJANAPPA (D) BY LRS. & ANR.         Appellant(s)
                                VERSUS
A. THIPPESWAMY & ORS.                     Respondent(s)
O R D E R
The appellants before us are not only the legal
heirs of the defendant No.1, but also seek to canvass
their independent rights as the children born out of
the wedlock between defendant No.1 and his second
wife Hanumakka @ Hanumanthamma.
The respondent Nos.1 to 7 are the plaintiffs in
the suit. The suit was filed for partition and
separate possession against the defendant No.1, who
is the father of plaintiff No.1. It is the say of
defendant No.1 that during the subsistence of his
first marriage with Bassamma, he married her sister –
Hanumakka @ Hanumanthamma. It is the further case of
defendant No.1 that the second marriage took place
prior to the coming into force of the Hindu Marriage
Act, 1956 (for short ‘the 1956 Act’). However, the
Trial Court gave a finding that the marriage was
subsequent to the 1956 Act i.e. in the year 1966 and,
hence,  concluded  that  the  second  wife  and  her
children were not necessary parties to the suit.

--- Page 228 ---
2
Consequently, the Trial Court decreed the suit on the
premise that the suit properties are ancestral in
nature.  
Aggrieved, the appellants preferred a regular
first appeal before the High Court and filed two
applications seeking to implead themselves as parties
in the pending first appeal, and to mark documents to
substantiate the fact that the marriage between the
defendant No.1 and their mother took place much prior
to the coming into force of the 1956 Act. However,
the said applications were taken up along with the
first appeal and were dismissed by the High Court.
Aggrieved by the same, the present appeal has
been filed. 
Learned  Senior  counsel  appearing  for  the
appellant(s) would submit that the High Court has
completely erred in rejecting the two impleadment
applications, especially, when there is no dispute
with respect to the factum of the second marriage and
the appellants being the children born out of the
wedlock between defendant No.1 and Hanumakka. The
finding by the Trial Court, as confirmed by the High
Court, with respect to the date of marriage, cannot
be made binding on the appellants, as they were not
made parties before the Trial Court and the documents
which they sought to rely upon were not even looked
into at the relevant point of time.

--- Page 229 ---
3
Learned counsel appearing for the respondent(s)-
plaintiffs would submit that, as rightly observed by
the High Court, the appellants are only entitled for
a share out of the one allotted to the defendant
No.1, being the illegitimate children, in accordance
with  the  law  as  laid  down  by  this  Court  in
Revanasiddappa  and  Anr.  v.  Mallikarjun  and  Ors.
(2023) 10 SCC 1.
Upon hearing the learned senior counsel and the
learned counsel for the parties, we are not in a
position to give our imprimatur to the judgment of
the High Court.
Admittedly, the appellants have not been heard,
especially in the sense that they have sought to mark
some documents and assert their independent rights
over the subject properties.  It is not in dispute
that the defendant no.1 has married the sister of his
first  wife  Bassamma,  namely,  Hanumakka  @
Hanumanthamma, who is the mother of the appellants.
The findings rendered  by both the Courts inter
se  the plaintiffs and the defendant No.1 cannot be
made binding on the appellants, who have got their
independent  rights  to  agitate  qua  the  suit
properties.
The plaintiffs – respondent(s) knew about the
presence of the appellants. The appellants also,
admittedly, have tried to mark the relevant documents

--- Page 230 ---
4
before the High Court to substantiate the fact that
the marriage of the defendant No.1 – Anjanappa and
Hanumakka took place before coming into force of the
1956 Act. 
In  such  view  of  the  matter,  we  allow  the
applications  filed  by  the  appellants  seeking  to
implead themselves as parties in the regular first
appeal before the High Court. The documents sought to
be filed and relied upon are directed to be marked,
subject to admissibility, relevancy and proof.
The High Court is at liberty to call for a
finding  from  the  concerned  Trial  Court,  by
facilitating  taking  and  recording  of  necessary
evidence on the issue of date and year of the
defendant No.1 – Anjanappa's second marriage, by
considering  the  relevant  oral  and  documentary
evidence.
In such view of the matter, the impugned order
stands set aside and the matter stands remitted to
the High Court for fresh consideration.
The appeal stands allowed, in the aforesaid
terms.
We request the High Court to dispose of the
regular first appeal within a period of 1 year from
the date of receipt of a copy of this order.
All contentions are left open.
In the meantime, no third party rights shall be

          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. Heard Mr. Smarhar Singh, learned counsel for the
petitioners and  Mr. Akshay Amritanshu, learned counsel for
1

--- Page 246 ---
the  respondent-State  and  Mr.  Sahil  Shandilya,  learned
counsel for respondent No.2.
2. The present Special leave Petition calls the final
judgment  and  order  dated  09.10.2025  in  Criminal
Miscellaneous No.42606/2024 passed by the High Court of
Judicature at Patna.
3. The petitioners are four in number. They are two
sisters and brothers-in-law or individual by name Aamir who
married respondent No.2-Farheen. An FIR was registered
bearing  No.312/2022  on  16.12.2022  alleging  offences
punishable under Section 498-A read with Section 34 of
Indian Penal Code, 1860 (for short “IPC”) and Sections 3
and 4 of the Dowry Prohibition Act. The petitioners filed
an application to quash the First Information Report.
4. The High Court has passed the following impugned
order:
 “No one appears on behalf of the petitioners.
2. Heard learned counsel appearing on behalf of the
opposite party no.2 and learned APP for the State.
3. The present application has been filed under
Section 482 Cr.P.C. for quashing of the order dated
29.01.2024 passed in Kako P.S. Case No. 312 of 2022
by the learned SDJM, Jehanabad, whereby cognizance
has been taken under Sections 341, 323, 504, 506
and 498A/34 of the IPC and Sections 3/4 of the
Dowry Prohibition Act.
4. Allegation against the petitioners is that the
husband of the opposite party no.2 is working
outside the country and taking advantage of the
said situation, the petitioners who are in-laws of
the opposite party no.2 subjected her to various
sorts of torture due to non-fulfillment of demand
of dowry.
2

--- Page 247 ---
5. Learned counsel appearing on behalf of the
opposite party no.2 submitted that after marriage,
the opposite party no.2 has been left to live her
life alone and leaving the opposite party no.2
alone by her husband is itself a cruelty. Today, no
one appeared on behalf of the petitioners after
obtaining interim protection by this Court vide
order dated 23.06.2025. He further submits that
opportunity  shall  be  given  to  the  parties  to
reconcile their dispute amicably.
6. Heard the parties.
7. In such circumstances, this Court finds it
proper that the opposite party no.2 may be given
opportunity to reconcile with the petitioners and
for that the husband, namely, Aamir Khan must
participate to settle the dispute with his own
family members and keep the opposite party no.2
with  full  dignity  and  honour.  Any  sort  of
suppression without any legal steps taken will also
amount to cruelty.
8. Having considered the rival submissions made on
behalf of the parties, I find that the parties have
failed to settle the matrimonial dispute, the Court
till last minute must strive to give opportunity to
the parties to settle the dispute between the
husband and wife amicably. The matrimonial dispute
is not an offense against the society rather a
matrimonial dispute is a private conflict between
spouses  and  does  not  inherently  constitute  an
offence against society. However, a false case can
have a disastrous consequence in absence of any
criminal content. The personal dispute cannot call
for  a  criminal  offence.  Continuation  of  the
proceeding would amount to abuse of process of law
leading  to  vexatious  proceeding  against  the
petitioners.
9. In this regard, the Apex Court in the case of
B.S. Joshi v. State of Haryana, reported in, (2003)
4 SCC 675, in paragraph nos. 12 and 13 has held as
under:-
"12. The special features in such matrimonial
matters are evident. It becomes the duty of the
court  to  encourage  genuine  settlements  of
matrimonial disputes.
13. The observations made by this Court, though
in a slightly different context, in G. V. Rao v.
L.H. V. Prasad /(2000) 3 SCC 693 : 2000 SCC
(Cri) 733) are very apt for determining the
3

--- Page 248 ---
approach required to be kept in view in a
matrimonial dispute by the courts. It was said
that there has been an outburst of matrimonial
disputes in recent times. Marriage is a sacred
ceremony, the main purpose of which is to enable
the young couple to settle down in life and live
peacefully. But little matrimonial skirmishes
suddenly  erupt  which  often  assume  serious
proportions resulting in commission of heinous
crimes in which elders of the family are also
involved with the result that those who could
have counselled and brought about rapprochement
are rendered helpless on their being arrayed as
accused in the criminal case. There are many
other reasons which need not be mentioned here
for not encouraging matrimonial litigation so
that the parties may ponder over their defaults
and terminate their disputes amicably by mutual
agreement instead of fighting it out in a court
of  law  where  it  takes  years  and  years  to
conclude and in that process the parties lose
their "young" days in chasing their "cases" in
different courts.”
10. Both the parties are directed to appear before
the learned District Court on 19.11.2025 at 10:30
AM.
11. Learned District Court is directed to take
necessary steps to refer the matter before the
learned Mediator of the District Mediation Center:
12. Learned Mediator of the District Mediation
Center concerned shall make his/her best efforts
to  settle  the  dispute  amicably  and  thereafter
submit his/her report before the concerned learned
District  Court,  well  within  a  period  of  four
months, till then, no coercive action shall be
taken against the petitioners in connection with
the aforesaid case.
13.  In  case  of  failure  on  the  part  of  the
petitioners to appear on 19.11.2025 before the
learned District Court or any date fixed by the
learned Mediator, the interim protection granted
to the petitioners shall automatically lose its
force.
14. In case, the parties fail to reconcile, then in
that case, the learned District Court shall proceed
with the trial.
4

--- Page 249 ---
15. In case, the parties resolve their dispute
amicably, then the proceeding is required to be
dropped in light of the law laid down by the Apex
Court as referred hereinabove.
16. Accordingly, the present quashing application
stands disposed of.”
5. We find from the High Court’s order that there are no
consideration of the contentions on merits. All that has
been set out is that, the Court gave an opportunity for the
husband who was not the party to settle the dispute with
full dignity and honour and thereafter the High Court has
ordered that having failed to settle, the High Court was of
the opinion that the interim order granted should be
vacated. Immediately thereafter the High Court records that
in case the parties fail to reconcile, the trial has to
proceed and thereafter the quash petition itself has been
disposed of.
6. Since  we  noted  that  no  one  appeared  for  the
petitioners before the High Court, we are of the opinion
that the matter should be remitted back to the High Court
for fresh consideration.
7. The  impugned  order  is  set  aside.  The  Criminal
Miscellaneous No.42606/2024 stands restored on the file of
the High Court. The prayer(s) of the petitioners are
allowed. The Special Leave Petition is disposed of. Any
interim order that obtained during the pendency of the
appeal, shall continue.
5

--- Page 250 ---
8. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed
of.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CIVIL APPEAL  NO.         OF 2026
(@ SLP(C) No. 4079/2026)
LATE MOTIRAM NAIK SHIKSHAN 
SANSTHA VITHALA & ANR.  APPELLANT(s)
                                VERSUS
THE EDUCATION OFFICER (SECONDARY) & ORS.        RESPONDENT(S)
O R D E R
1. Leave granted. 
2. We have heard the learned Senior Counsel appearing
for the appellant and the learned counsel appearing
for the respondents.
3. In pursuance of the charges framed and, thereafter,
proved by the departmental inquiry, the respondent
no.3 was removed from the services. The Tribunal,
inter  alia,  held that the principles of natural
justice having not been followed in examining the
material witnesses, hence, the charge against the
respondent  No.3  has  not  been  substantiated  and
proved. The said view was concurred with by the High
Court. 

--- Page 272 ---
2
4. Upon hearing the learned Senior Counsel appearing
for the respondents, we are inclined to set aside
the impugned order on the sole premise that in the
event of such a finding, the entire benefit cannot
be granted in favour of the respondent(s), as the
concept of the principle of natural justice has got
two facets. Firstly, non-following it would vitiate
the very proceedings themselves, and the other is
the question of prejudice. 
5. The Tribunal and the High Court having found that
the witnesses have not been examined, ought to have
remitted the matter for fresh consideration. In
other words, non-compliance with the principles of
natural justice in not examining the witnesses will
not  amount  to  giving  a  clean-chit  to  the
respondent(s).  Needless  to  state  that  in  a
departmental  inquiry,  it  is  for  department  to
substantiate the charge.
6. In such view of the matter, while not interfering
with the reinstatement of the respondent No.3, we
give liberty to the appellant to proceed afresh in
pursuance of the charges framed. 
7. The inquiry, if any, to be proceeded with, shall be
done leaving all the issues open. We make it clear
that respondent No.3 shall be reinstated.

--- Page 273 ---
3
8. The appeal stands disposed of, in the aforesaid
terms with the aforementioned observations. 
9. Pending application(s), if any, shall also stand
disposed of.

   [M.M. SUNDRESH]

SLP (Crl.) No.9882/2026                              1

--- Page 292 ---
the following observations:-
Learned counsel appearing for the respondent-State
would submit that out of 80 witnesses cited in the

5. A perusal of the aforestated order would indicate

for grant of bail after three months. It is now stated by the
learned counsel appearing for the respondent-State that
out of 23 eye-witnesses 14 have been examined and the
remaining witnesses are yet to be examined and it would
take further time of at least two to three months. The
witnesses hitherto examined have not supported the case
of the prosecution. The role attributed to the appellant is
that he was a conspirator and had extended his logistical
support and had participated in the meetings held before
the occurrence and thereby, had facilitated the crime.

--- Page 293 ---
6. In the light of the fact that the witnesses examined

and the appellant being in custody till date from the date

warranted. Hence, we allow this appeal, set aside the
impugned order and grant regular bail to the appellant.

conditions as it deems fit, in the instant case. Accordingly,
the appeal stands allowed.

                   Ms. Farah Hashmi, Adv.

                             O R D E R
Heard Mr. Siddharth Dave, learned Senior Counsel for the
petitioners, Mr. Siddharth Luthra, learned Senior Counsel for the
respondents no.1 to 4 and Mr. Balbir Singh, learned Senior Counsel
for the respondent no.6.
2.  The present petition has been filed against the impugned
order dated 05.03.2025 passed by the High Court of Judicature at
Bombay at Nagpur Bench in Criminal Writ Petition No.887 of 2019, by
which the petition filed by the petitioners seeking a CBI inquiry
and other ancillary reliefs, has been dismissed observing that in
case, if appropriate evidence is brought to the notice of the
learned Trial Judge in the matter of an offence being committed by
the Directors of the respondents no.6 and 7-Companies, the same
shall be dealt with by the learned Trial Judge in accordance with
the provisions of Sections 216 and 319 of the Code of Criminal
Procedure, 1973 (hereinafter referred to as  the “Cr.P.C.”) or in
accordance with other provisions of law.
3. Learned Senior Counsel for the petitioners submitted that the
land belonging to the petitioners was illegally excavated by the
respondents no.6 and 7 and used for building its project under a
contract, which the respondent no.6 had with the Government for
building the Nagpur-Mumbai Expressway. It was submitted that the

--- Page 298 ---
3
said act of the respondents no.6 and 7 was illegal mainly on two
counts. Firstly, that no permission or agreement existed between
the petitioners and the respondents no.6 and 7 for such excavation
and secondly, that no permission was taken from the appropriate
authorities under the relevant Statutes for excavating the earth
from the place from which, it has been done.
4. Learned Senior Counsel for the petitioners further submitted
that pursuant to their complaint, an FIR was lodged, but only under
the provisions of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 (hereinafter referred
to as the “IPC”) and not under the Mines and Minerals (Development
and Regulation) Act, 1957 (hereinafter referred to as the “MMDR
Act”) or under any other statutory provisions including the Indian
Forest Act, 1927 (hereinafter referred to as the “Forest Act”). It
was contended that the High Court giving an observation in its
impugned order that if any appropriate evidence shall be brought to
the notice of the Trial Judge, then based on the same, the Trial
Court would act keeping in mind the provisions of Sections 216 and
319 of the Cr.P.C., is meaningless for the reason that it is the
prosecution agency to bring on record evidence and the entire
prosecution is directed only under the IPC thus, there cannot be
any occasion for any evidence other than what the prosecution has
brought on record in the charge sheet, which would be produced
before the Trial Court. It was further contended that besides
causing  personal  loss  to  the  petitioners,  the  act  of  the
respondents no.6 and 7 has resulted in damage to the environment
and to the ecology as earth/gravel/trees have also been removed
from forest land and thus, at least, the State of Maharashtra

--- Page 299 ---
4
should have been more vigilant in the matter, which it has not
been.
5. Learned Senior Counsel for the respondents no.1 to 4 drew the
attention of the Court to paragraph no.17 of the impugned order,
where  it  has  been  noted  that  the  learned  Additional  Public
Prosecutor has taken a categorical stand that issue with regard to
non-invoking of Section 23 of the MMDR Act will be looked into and
if so required by the Trial Court at an appropriate stage can issue
directions or else if so required, a supplementary charge sheet can
be submitted to that effect.
6. Learned Senior Counsel for the respondent no.6 has adopted the
arguments of the learned Senior Counsel for the respondents no.1 to
4.
7. Having considered the matter, we find that the issue raised by
the petitioners is of great importance and is not being negated or
shot down by the impugned order. The primary concern is that
whoever commits any offence under the relevant Statues, both the
MMDR Act as well as the Forest Act and the general penal Statutes
of the country, is liable to be prosecuted thereunder. Thus, taking
into consideration the fact that a window has been given in the
impugned order and also the stand taken before the Court on behalf
of the State of Maharashtra, the present petition stands disposed
of by clarifying that the State of Maharashtra shall look into the
matter and take a decision with regard to whatever offence is made
out against all the concerned person(s)/respondents under the MMDR
Act, the Forest Act as well as the general penal Statues and
accordingly, as a consequence, do the needful as may be required,

--- Page 300 ---
5
both by way of further investigation and also by submitting
supplementary charge sheet before the Trial Court, which shall be
considered in accordance with law. We further give liberty to the
petitioners to participate in the trial and to adduce evidence
because of the fact that from their land also, the earth has been
excavated. 
8. Before parting, as we have been informed that on the same
issue, the respondent no.6 has moved before the High Court of
Judicature at Bombay at Nagpur Bench in Writ Petition No.415 of
2020, Crl. Application No.372 of 2020 and Writ Petition No.2185 of
2020 in which, there are interim orders and the said petitions are
pending, we request the High Court to dispose of the same within
six months. As the matter is of great importance, in case the High
Court is unable to dispose of the said petitions within six months,
the stay granted in such proceedings shall automatically stand
vacated and consequences thereof shall follow. We expect that in
view of the fact that witnesses are already being examined before
the Trial Court, the State of Maharashtra is required to take
necessary action expeditiously. Learned Senior Counsel for the
respondents no.1 to 4 assures us of the same.
9. Pending application(s), if any, shall also stand disposed of.
(SAPNA BISHT)                                   (ANJALI PANWAR)
COURT MASTER (SH)                             ASSISTANT  REGISTRAR

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CRIMINAL APPEAL No.            /2026
[@ SPECIAL LEAVE PETITION (CRL.) NO.13991/2026]
KADAPALA RAMESH                      Appellant(s)
                      VERSUS
THE STATE OF ANDHRA PRADESH          Respondent(s)
 O R D E R
1. Leave granted.
2. Heard learned counsel for the parties.
3. This  appeal  arises  from  an  order  dated
27.04.2026 passed by the Andhra Pradesh High Court
rejecting the application of the appellant seeking
suspension of sentence awarded by the Trial Court.
4. At the outset, the learned counsel for the
appellant  submits  that  the  case  against  the
appellant  is  based  entirely  on  circumstantial
evidence, and an extra-judicial confession. The
circumstantial  evidence  is  in  respect  of  the
deceased being last seen at the shop of the
appellant.  However,  such  circumstance  is  not
clinching since the body of the deceased was found
Crl.A. @ SLP (Crl.) No. 13991/2026                    1

--- Page 337 ---
next day after a gap of several hours and at a
place much away from the place where he was last
seen together with the appellant. There is also
evidence of recovery of a rope allegedly used for
strangulating the deceased.   However, the same
could not be linked to the crime and witnesses set
up to prove its acquisition by the accused have
been declared hostile. In such circumstances, it
is submitted there is hardly any evidence on which
conviction  could  be  sustained.  Besides,  the
appellant has already served more than 3 years of
sentence and there is no likelihood of his appeal
being heard in near future.
5. The learned counsel for the State has opposed
the prayer for suspension of sentence. However, he
could  not  dispute  that  the  case  against  the
appellant  is  based  on  circumstances  narrated
above.  He has also not been able to show that the
appellant has prior criminal history. 
6.  Having  regard  to  the  nature  of  evidence
available  against  the  appellant,  without
Crl.A. @ SLP (Crl.) No. 13991/2026                    2

--- Page 338 ---
expressing any opinion on the merits of the appeal
pending before the High Court, we are of the view
that the appellant is entitled for suspension of
sentence  pending  consideration  of  his  appeal
before the High Court.
7. The appeal is, accordingly, allowed. The order
of the High Court rejecting the bail prayer of the
appellant is set aside. The sentence awarded to
the appellant by the Trial Court shall remain
suspended pending consideration of his appeal by
the High Court.
8. Pending disposal of his appeal by the High
Court, the appellant shall be released on bail on
such terms and conditions as the trial court may
deem fit to impose.
9. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand
disposed of.

[MANOJ MISRA]
……………………………………………………J
New Delhi                          [VIJAY BISHNOI]

(Arising out of SLP (CRL) No. 264/2026)
C.A. SASI                                           Appellant(s)
                                VERSUS
STATE OF KERALA & ANR.                             
R-1: State of Kerala
R-2: Deputy Superintendent of Police
Vigilance And Anti- Corruption Bureau,
Thiruvananthapuram-695021, Kerala State
 
   Respondent(s)
O R D E R
Heard Mr. Kaleeswaram Raj, learned counsel for the petitioner
and Mr. Zulfiker Ali P. S., learned counsel for the respondent
No.1-State of Kerala. 
2. Leave granted.
3. The appellant was sentenced to undergo rigorous imprisonment
for two years and to pay a fine of Rs. 1,00,000/- (Rupees One Lakh)
and,  in  default  of  payment  of  fine,  to  undergo  rigorous
imprisonment for three months under Section 13(1)(c) read with
Section 13(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988; he was
also sentenced to undergo rigorous imprisonment for one year and to
pay a fine of Rs. 10,000/- (Rupees Ten Thousand) and, in default of
payment of fine, to undergo rigorous imprisonment for two months

--- Page 352 ---
2
under Section 409 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 (hereinafter
referred to as the “IPC”); and he was further sentenced  to undergo
rigorous  imprisonment  for  six  months  and  to  pay  a  fine  of
Rs.10,000/- (Rupees Ten Thousand) and, in default of payment of
fine, to undergo rigorous imprisonment for two months under Section
477-A of IPC. The substantive sentences were ordered to run
concurrently.
4. Learned counsel for the appellant draws our attention to the
order  of  this  Court  dated  12.01.2026  passed  in  the  present
proceedings and submits that the Court had noted that the appellant
was ready to deposit a further amount of Rs.1,00,000/- (Rupees One
Lakh) to compensate the State exchequer for the loss suffered by
the State, which at the relevant point of time was assessed at
Rs.1,00,000/- (Rupees One Lakh), over and above what has been
awarded by the Court . It was submitted that the sentence may be
reduced to the minimum period prescribed at the relevant point of
time, i.e., one year imprisonment. It was submitted that the
appellant is in custody since 27.12.2025, i.e., almost nine months.
5. Learned counsel for the respondent No. 1-State  submits that
the loss suffered by the State exchequer was Rs.1,00,000/- (Rupees
One Lakh) in the year 1999. Thus, it was submitted that if the
Court is inclined to interfere, the amount  to be paid by the
appellant  over  and  above  the  amount  already  imposed may  be
substantial.
6. Having considered the matter in its entirety and going through

--- Page 353 ---
3
the material on record, we find that the ends of justice will be
served if the appellant deposits Rs.2,00,000/- (Rupees Two Lakhs)
in total, including the fine imposed by the Trial Court and as
upheld by the High Court.
7. In view thereof, while upholding the conviction, we modify the
sentence  awarded  to  one  year  imprisonment  and  the  fine  to
Rs.2,00,000/- (Rupees Two Lakhs) . The fine be deposited within one
month. The appellant would be released on completion of a period of
one year of incarceration.
8. The appeal stands partly allowed in the aforementioned terms.
9. Pending applications, if any, stand disposed of.

Chief Judicial Magistrate, Nagpur, Maharashtra is transferred
to the Court of the Chief Judicial Magistrate, Bhavnagar,
Gujarat.

given in all the matters pending between the parties so as to
enable them to appear in all the cases on a single day instead
of different dates.

that two persons were selling drugs and on intercepting a Tata Safari, they
found 17 bottles of cough syrup and Rs.5,000/- was allegedly recovered
from the co-accused Iftekhar Khan and appellant produced 13 strips of
Proxiohm-Spas capsules, 104 capsules in total (amounting to 5.2 gms of
Tramadol) and as such both of them were arrested. After completion of
investigation, chargesheet has been filed. Two out of fourteen witnesses
have been examined.
1                                                                                    SLP(CRL.) NO.14747 OF 2026

--- Page 378 ---
5. As could be seen from the charge-sheet material, the quantity of
contraband that came to be seized from the appellant was 5.2 gms of
Tramadol tablets, which is less than commercial quantity, namely,
intermediate quantity. Having regard to the same and also the fact there
are no other criminal antecedents attributable to the appellant and the fact
that the appellant has already spent around seven months in custody, we
are of the considered view that appellant is entitled for being released on
bail.
6.  Hence, we allow the appeal. Set aside the impugned order and direct
the appellant to be released on regular bail on such terms and conditions
as the jurisdictional trial court may deem fit to impose.
7. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of.

1. We have heard Mr. K. M. Nataraj, learned Additional Solicitor
General and Mr. Mamidipudi Venkatarama Mukunda, learned Amici
Curiae.
2. We are of the opinion that two steps need to be taken to
ensure the implementation of the principle that wherever there is a
road, there must be a footpath.
3. We direct the Union of India to identify an Authority, which
would be responsible for implementing the need for establishing the
footpaths.  Such an authority, if not in existence or identifiable
within the statutory framework of any Statute, then such an
Authority can be established.  It is necessary for such an
Authority to have the necessary wherewithal in terms of the space,
infrastructure, human resources and funds.
4. Mr. K. M. Nataraj will report to the Court on the next date of
hearing about identification of such Authority, which will take
responsibility and implement the scheme.
5. We are of the opinion that at least 05 Towns can be identified
in the country to start a pilot project for provisioning footpaths
wherever the road exists.  Mr. Nataraj will take instructions and

--- Page 388 ---
4
apprise this Court on the next date of hearing about the places
where the pilot project can be implemented.
6. Re-list the matter on 06.11.2026.

Civil Appeal No.13319 of 2026 
Page 1 of 4 
 
 
IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA 
CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION  
 
CIVIL APPEAL NO.13319 OF 2026 
 
KALLU KHAN                            APPELLANT 
VERSUS 
DISTRICT EDUCATION OFFICER         RESPONDENT 
 
O R D E R 
 
1. We are in this Civil Appeal concerned with the correctness of 
the order dated 11.02.2026 passed by the Division Bench of the 
Rajasthan High Court 1 in D.B. Review Petition (Writ) No.31 of 
2026. By the said order, the Division Bench declined to recall its 
earlier order dated 04.08.2025 by which it modified the relief that 
was granted to the appellant, in the form of a direction for 
reinstatement with continuity in service and payment of 50 
percent backwages with lumpsum monetary compensation of 
₹5,00,000/-.  
2. Pursuant to liberty granted to the appellant to raise a dispute 
under the provisions of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 2, for 
 
1 For short, ‘the High Court’ 
2 For short, ‘the Act of 1947’ 

--- Page 406 ---
 
Civil Appeal No.13319 of 2026 
Page 2 of 4 
 
seeking redressal of his grievance that his services as a contractual 
daily wager had been unlawfully terminated, the appellant filed a 
dispute under Section 2A(2) of the Act of 1947. The Labour Court 
passed an award on 18.02.2020 and directed his reinstatement in 
service with continuity, full backwages and other consequential 
benefits. In the writ petition preferred by the respondent, a learned 
Single Judge of the High Court on 05.03.2021 , partly allowed the 
said writ petition and modified the award passed by the Labour 
Court. While maintaining the direction to reinstate the appellant, 
the backwages were reduced from 100 per cent to 50 per cent. In 
the writ appeal preferred by the respondent, the Division Bench by 
its order dated 04.08.2025, substituted the relief of reinstatement 
and grant of 50 per cent backwages with the relief of monetary 
compensation of ₹5,00,000/-. 
3. The appellant challenged the order dated 04.08.2025 before 
this Court by filing SLP(C) No.34608 of 2025. On 12.12.2025, this 
Court declined to interfere with the impugned order under Article 
136 of the Constitution of India. The special leave petition was 
dismissed with liberty to the appellant to take appropriate steps 
that may be available in law. Pursuant to the aforesaid order, the 
appellant sought review of the order dated 04.08.2025, passed by 

--- Page 407 ---
 
Civil Appeal No.13319 of 2026 
Page 3 of 4 
 
the Division Bench. The review petition preferred by the appellant 
was, however, dismissed on 11.02.2026. It is this order that the 
appellant has sought to challenge in the present appeal. On 
18.06.2026, this Court had issued notice in the present 
proceedings. Despite service, the respondent did not choose to 
contest the appeal. Hence, on 24.09.2026, the respondent was set 
ex-parte. In the aforesaid backdrop, the learned counsel for the 
appellant was heard.  
4. Having considered the material on record, it is seen that the 
order dated 04.08.2025 passed by the Division Bench in special 
writ appeal by which monetary compensation of ₹5,00,000/- was 
awarded to the appellant in lieu of reinstatement in service was  
unsuccessfully challenged by the appellant  before this Court.  It 
would, therefore, not be permissible for this Court to again re -
examine the correctness of the order dated 04.08.2025. The order 
dated 11.02.2026 rejecting the recall application also does not call 
for interference. However, in the peculiar facts of the present case, 
it is seen that the appellant had served as a contractual daily wager 
from 19.11.1990 to 01.09.1998 . Coupled with the fact that the 
appellant was pursuing his remedies since 10.09.1998 which 
culminated into the order dated 04.08.2025 and that, if reinstated, 

--- Page 408 ---
 
Civil Appeal No.13319 of 2026 
Page 4 of 4 
 
the appellant would have served for a period of three more years, 
we are of the view that award of monetary compensation of 
₹7,50,000/- would serve the ends of justice. We reiterate that this 
order is passed in the peculiar facts of the present case and same 
shall not be treated as a precedent. The aforesaid monetary 
compensation be paid to the appellant within a period of one 
month from today. The Civil Appeal is disposed of in the aforesaid 
terms. The pending Interlocutory Application is also disposed of.

               VERSUS

O R D E R
1. Leave granted.
2. We have heard Mr. Aditya Vaibhav Singh, learned
counsel for the appellant and Mr. Rahul K. Gupta, learned
counsel for the respondent-State of Bihar.
3. This  appeal  takes  exception  to  the  order  dated
24.02.2026, passed by the High Court of Judicature of
Patna (briefly the ‘High Court’ hereinafter) rejecting
the prayer for anticipatory bail made by the appellant.
4. Appellant has been named as an accused in Shastri
Nagar Police Station Case No.735 of 2025, registered
under Sections 115(2), 126(2), 109, 118(2) and 3(5) of
the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (for short, ‘BNS’). As
1

--- Page 414 ---
per the prosecution case, appellant had assaulted the
victim over a very trivial dispute causing grievous
injury.
5. This Court by order dated 13.04.2026, had issued
notice and in the meantime directed that no coercive
steps should be taken against the appellant provided he
joined investigation.
6. In the hearing today, learned State counsel fairly
submits that appellant has joined the investigation.
However, he has pointed to the grievous nature of the
injury suffered by the victim.
7. We have perused the materials on record wherefrom we
find that there was a fight between the two groups
leading to injuries on both the sides. Though no grievous
injury was found on the person of the victim, it was,
however, submitted before the Trial Court that he had
suffered grievous injury at the hands of the appellant.
We  also  find  that  appellant  also  suffered  several
injuries on his person including fracture on his left
forearm.
8. That being the position and considering the fact that
appellant has joined investigation, we are inclined to
grant anticipatory bail to the appellant.
9. Consequently, impugned order of the High Court dated
24.02.2026 is set aside and our order dated 13.04.2026 is
made absolute subject to the condition that appellant
shall continue to cooperate with the investigation.
2

--- Page 415 ---
10. Appeal is accordingly allowed.
11. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed
of.
